name: The Changing-Lines Lens
description: The I Ching read one line and one direction at a time. It starts with the fifth line, the ruler's place, turning from yang to yin: what the tradition says about the six places, the four trigrams that lose their middle, the 32 solid fifth lines and the 32 broken ones they become, and how often a cast lands there. An appendix holds all twelve tables (six places, two directions, 32 hexagrams each). Draft.

sections.Reading: What does it mean for yang to turn into yin in the fifth line, in all the hexagrams where that can happen? This course holds that one place and that one movement still and reads all 32 cases. You will read what the tradition says about the fifth place, see which trigrams change, read the line texts on both sides of the change, and count how often a cast lands there. A reading doesn't tell you your fate; it might help you create it.

nodes.name: What the tradition says about the six places

sections.Reading:
The line texts of the Zhouyi do not explain themselves. The explanations of place come from the commentaries bound with the book, the Ten Wings, and from the readers who followed them. Four ideas carry most of the weight.

Correct and incorrect places. Legge puts the rule plainly: "The first, the third, and the fifth lines in a hexagram, if they are 'correct' as it is called, should all be whole, and the second, fourth, and sixth lines should all be divided" [@legge_intro]. A solid fifth line is in its correct place; a broken one is not.

The centre. Lines 2 and 5 are the middle lines of the two trigrams. In Legge's words they "have a peculiar value and force" [@legge_intro]. The Small Images of the Ten Wings use the centre often to explain why a line is fortunate: of the 32 solid fifth lines, the Small Image names the centre or the due mean for 13 of them [@legge_appendices].

Correlates. Lines 1 and 4, 2 and 5, 3 and 6 answer each other, best when one is solid and the other broken. Legge: "Let the subject of the fifth be the sovereign or a commander-in-chief, according to the name and meaning of the hexagram, then the subject of the second will be an able minister or a skilful officer" [@legge_intro]. So the fifth place is the ruler's place, and the second is the place of the one who serves.

The noble place. The Great Commentary compares the places in pairs. Of the third and the fifth it says: 三多凶，五多功，貴賤之等也 [@xici_ws]; in Legge, "the third meets with many misfortunes, while the occupant of the fifth achieves much merit:—this arises from one being in the noble position and the other in the mean." It goes on: "Are they occupied by the symbol of weakness? There will be peril. By that of strength? There will be victory" [@legge_app3]. Read literally, a solid fifth line turning broken moves from victory toward peril. The next chapters test how far the line texts bear that out.

The ruler of the hexagram. Wang Bi (226-249) argued that a hexagram is governed by one line: the commentary on the judgment 統論一卦之體，明其所由之主者也, sets out the whole figure and makes clear the ruler it comes from. Without the central lines, he wrote, nothing would be complete (非其中爻，莫之備矣), and where five lines are yang and one is yin, the yin line rules (一卦五陽而一陰，則一陰為之主矣) [@wangbi]. Richard John Lynn translated Wang Bi's commentary into English in 1994 [@lynn1994]. Much later, Li Guangdi, who edited the imperial Zhouyi zhezhong of 1715, distinguished a ruler that forms the hexagram from a ruler that governs it [@zhezhong_study]. Richard J. Smith's history of the book traces how these schools of reading grew [@smith2008].

sections.Reading:
A line can only change into its opposite. A cast that moves it turns the first figure into a second one, the relating hexagram, and the line text of the first figure is the one a reader reads.

A fifth line is the middle line of the upper trigram. Only four trigrams have a solid middle line: Qian 乾 (Heaven, three solid lines), Kan 坎 (Water, solid between two broken), Xun 巽 (Wind, broken below two solid) and Dui 兌 (Lake, broken above two solid). Each sits on top of each of the eight trigrams once, which gives the 32.

When the fifth line turns, the upper trigram loses its solid middle:

Qian becomes Li 離, Heaven becomes Fire.
Kan becomes Kun 坤, Water becomes Earth.
Xun becomes Gen 艮, Wind becomes Mountain.
Dui becomes Zhen 震, Lake becomes Thunder.

Gen is not among them: Mountain has a broken middle line (one solid line on top), so its fifth line, when it sits above, is broken already. It appears on the other side, as a trigram the change arrives at.

The Shuogua, the eighth Wing, gives the trigrams a family: Qian the father, Kun the mother, Zhen, Kan and Gen the oldest, middle and youngest sons, Xun, Li and Dui the oldest, middle and youngest daughters [@legge_app5]. Each trigram's place in the family is set by its one odd line, so this change crosses the family each time: the father becomes the middle daughter, the middle son becomes the mother, the oldest daughter becomes the youngest son, and the youngest daughter becomes the oldest son. In family terms, a solid fifth line turning broken never keeps the upper trigram's gender.

sections.Reading:
These are the texts a reader meets when the fifth line of the cast is a 9. Read together, a few threads recur. None runs through all 32.

A ruler, or someone in the ruler's seat. The great man appears in 1 (the dragon on the wing), 12 (the one who brings the standstill to a close) and 49 (the tiger changing his stripes); a king in 8 (the hunt that lets the game escape) and 37 (the king's influence reaching his family); the one who scatters the royal granaries in 59; the one who sets regulations sweetly in 60; the union of all under one in 45.

Sincerity. The word 孚, sincerity or trust, appears in 7 of the 32 solid fifth lines, more than in any other place and polarity [@lens_script]: in 9 and 61 (sincere, drawing others to him), 17 (sincere in what is excellent), 42 (with sincere heart seeking to benefit all below), 45, 49 (trusted before he divines) and 58, where the trust goes to one who would injure him.

Difficulty met from the centre. Several solid fifth lines sit in hard times and hold: 3 (difficulty in giving out favours), 29 (the water of the defile not yet full), 39 (the greatest difficulties, while friends are coming), 47 (nose and feet cut off, and yet at ease) and 63 (the neighbour's small sacrifice outweighing the great one).

Peril in the right place. Two lines warn while the Small Image calls the place correct: 10 ("Though he be firm and correct, there will be peril") and 58 ("The situation is perilous"). For 10 the Small Image puts the peril down to "his being in the position that is correct and appropriate to him" [@legge_appendices]. A strong line in the strong place can be too much of one thing.

The verdict words: 吉 appears in 12 of the 32 solid fifth lines, and 凶 in 1 of the 32 (hexagram 3: "good fortune in small things; (even) with them in great things there will be evil") [@zhouyi_core].

nodes.name: Where they go: the broken fifth lines

sections.Reading:
The relating hexagram is where the cast points. Its own fifth line is now broken, and though a reader following Zhu Xi's rule reads only the first figure's line [@cottrell_chuhsi], the new fifth line shows what kind of place the change opens. Read across the 32 relating hexagrams, one thread is strong: the ruler who receives rather than holds.

In 14 the ruler's sincerity is "reciprocated by that of all the others". In 11 and 54 the king gives his younger sister in marriage, the high going down to the low. In 2 the fifth line is a yellow lower garment, the colour of the centre worn below. In 38 the ruler unites with his minister "as if he were biting through a piece of skin"; in 15 he "without being rich, is able to employ his neighbours"; in 55 he brings "around him the men of brilliant ability"; in 41 others add to his stores and will not be refused; in 4 he is "a simple lad without experience", and the Small Image credits "his docility going on to humility" [@zhouyi_core; @legge_appendices]. This is the correlate Legge describes, turned round: a broken fifth line and a solid second, the soft ruler served by a strong minister [@legge_intro].

Two smaller threads: repentance disappearing (38, 35 and 52; and no repentance in 24, 34 and 64), and yellow, the central colour, in 2, 21 (yellow gold) and 50 (the caldron's yellow ears).

The Great Commentary expects weakness in the fifth place to mean peril [@legge_app3]. The line texts lean the other way on the rough count: 吉 appears in 17 of the 32 broken fifth lines, against 12 of the 32 solid ones. Taken pair by pair, in 7 of the 32 pairs both fifth lines carry 吉, in 10 only the broken one does, in 5 only the solid one, and in 10 neither.

So what does a solid fifth line turning broken do? Across the 32, the texts read less like a fall from the ruler's seat than like a change in how the seat is held: from holding the centre with firmness and sincerity, toward ruling by receiving, yielding and using the help of others. That is one reading of the pattern. Each case keeps its own text, and several (51, 16, 32, 7) speak of peril, illness or evil.

nodes.name: How often a cast lands here

sections.Reading:
By either method each line changes 1 in 4, and the fifth line is no different [@casting]. Which way it changes depends on the method. A 9 in the fifth place, a solid line about to turn broken, comes 1 in 8 with three coins and 3 in 16 with yarrow stalks. Put the other way: when the fifth line is solid, it moves 1 in 4 with coins and 3 in 8 with yarrow, because yarrow tilts toward moving solid lines.

The plainest case, the fifth line moving from yang and no other line moving, comes in 2.97% of coin casts and 4.45% of yarrow casts. Then Zhu Xi's rule is simple: read the changing line of the first figure [@cottrell_chuhsi]. Over a hundred yarrow readings, a reader might expect this case about four or five times, spread over 32 hexagrams.

The odds shape what comes up; they leave open what a reader does with it. [Casting and Chance](https://iching.recursive.eco/pages/course-viewer.html?course=casting-and-chance) sets out the methods and their odds in full.

sections.Reading:
The same lens works for every place. Hold a line and a direction still, read the 32 texts, and see what they share and where they part. The appendix holds all twelve tables, six places in two directions, built by a script from the public-domain texts in this repo [@lens_script]. Each gives the 32 hexagrams in King Wen order, the relating hexagram, the trigram that changes, Legge's line text and the Small Image.

Some places invite their own questions. Line 2 is the other centre, and the correlate of line 5: its tables can be read beside these. Line 3, where 吉 appears in only 6 of the 64 texts, is the hard place. Line 6 is the end of the figure, where 吉 and 凶 each appear in 17 of 64. Lines 1 to 3 change the lower trigram, the inner one; lines 4 to 6 the outer one.

A lens is a map, and a map is drawn for a purpose. This one was drawn to answer one question, about the ruler's place, and it gives a pattern in the texts, not a forecast. When a cast lands on one of these 32, the line text is still the one to read; the pattern only shows the company it keeps.
sections.Checked and claimed: The tables are built and checked by script ✔ [@lens_script]. The suggestions for other places are suggestions ◆.

sections.The line texts (Legge):
1 → 14. The Creative → Possession in Great Measure.
Line: In the fifth NINE, undivided, (we see its subject as) the dragon on the wing in the sky. It will be advantageous to meet with the great man.
Small Image: 'The dragon is on the wing in the sky:'—the great man rouses himself to his work.

3 → 24. Difficulty at the Beginning → Return (The Turning Point).
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows the difficulties in the way of (its subject's) dispensing the rich favours that might be expected from him. With firmness and correctness there will be good fortune in small things; (even) with them in great things there will be evil.
Small Image: 'Difficulty is experienced (by the subject of the fifth line) in bestowing his rich favours:'—the extent to which they reach will not yet be conspicuous.

5 → 11. Waiting (Nourishment) → Peace.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject waiting amidst the appliances of a feast. Through his firmness and correctness there will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The appliances of a feast, and the good fortune through being firm and correct,' are indicated by (the position in) the central and correct place.

6 → 64. Conflict → Before Completion.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject contending;—and with great good fortune.
Small Image: 'He contends;—and 'with great fortune:—this is shown by his holding the due mean and being in the correct place.

8 → 2. Holding Together [Union] → The Receptive.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, affords the most illustrious instance of seeking union and attachment. (We seem to see in it) the king urging his pursuit of the game (only) in three directions, and allowing the escape of all the animals before him, while the people of his towns do not warn one another (to prevent it). There will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The good fortune belonging to the most illustrious instance of seeking union and attachment' appears in the correct and central position (of the fifth line, undivided). (The king's) neglecting (the animals) confronting him (and then fleeing), and (only) taking those who present themselves as it were obediently, is seen in 'his allowing the escape of those in front of him.' 'That the people of his towns do not warn one another (to prevent such escape),' shows how he, in his high eminence, has made them pursue the due course.

9 → 26. The Taming Power of the Small → The Taming Power of the Great.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject possessed of sincerity, and drawing others to unite with him. Rich in resources, he employs his neighbours (in the same cause with himself).
Small Image: 'He is possessed of sincerity, and draws others to unite with him:'—he does not use only his own rich resources.

10 → 38. Treading [Conduct] → Opposition.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows the resolute tread of its subject. Though he be firm and correct, there will be peril.
Small Image: 'He treads resolutely; and though he be firm and correct, there is peril:'—this is due to his being in the position that is correct and appropriate to him.

12 → 35. Standstill [Stagnation] → Progress.
Line: In the fifth NINE, undivided, we see him who brings the distress and obstruction to a close,—the great man and fortunate. (But let him say), 'We may perish! We may perish!' (so shall the state of things become firm, as if) bound to a clump of bushy mulberry trees.
Small Image: The good fortune of the great man' arises from the correctness of his position.

13 → 30. Fellowship with Men → The Clinging, Fire.
Line: In the fifth NINE, undivided, (the representative of) the union of men first wails and cries out, and then laughs. His great host conquers, and he (and the subject of the second line) meet together.
Small Image: The first action of (the representative of) the union of men (here described) arises from his central position and straightforward character. 'The meeting secured by his great host' intimates that the opponents of it have been overcome.

17 → 51. Following → The Arousing (Shock, Thunder).
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows us (the ruler) sincere in (fostering all) that is excellent. There will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'He is sincere in fostering what is excellent:'—his position is correct and in the centre.

20 → 23. Contemplation [View] → Splitting Apart.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject contemplating his own life(-course). A superior man, he will (thus) fall into no error.
Small Image: 'He contemplates his own life(-course):'—he should (for this purpose) contemplate (the condition of) the people.

25 → 21. Innocence (The Unexpected) → Biting Through.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows one who is free from insincerity, and yet has fallen ill. Let him not use medicine, and he will have occasion for joy (in his recovery).
Small Image: 'Medicine in the case of one who is free from insincerity!'—it should not be tried (at all).

28 → 32. Preponderance of the Great → Duration.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows a decayed willow producing flowers, or an old wife in possession of her young husband. There will be occasion neither for blame nor for praise.
Small Image: 'A decayed willow produces flowers:'—but how can this secure its long continuance? 'An old wife and a young husband:'—this also is a thing to be ashamed of.

29 → 7. The Abysmal (Water) → The Army.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows the water of the defile not yet full, (so that it might flow away); but order will (soon) be brought about. There will be no error.
Small Image: 'The water in the defile is not full (so as to flow away):'—(the virtue indicated by) the central situation is not yet (sufficiently) great.

31 → 62. Influence (Wooing) → Preponderance of the Small.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows one moving the flesh along the spine above the heart. There will be no occasion for repentance.
Small Image: 'He (tries to) move the flesh along the spine above the heart:'—his aim is trivial.

33 → 56. Retreat → The Wanderer.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject retiring in an admirable way. With firm correctness there will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'He retires in an admirable way, and with firm correctness there will be good fortune:'—this is due to the rectitude of his purpose.

37 → 22. The Family [The Clan] → Grace.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows the influence of the king extending to his family. There need be no anxiety; there will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The influence of the king extends to his family:'—the intercourse between them is that of mutual love.

39 → 15. Obstruction → Modesty.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject struggling with the greatest difficulties, while friends are coming to help him.
Small Image: 'He struggles with the greatest difficulties, while friends are coming (to help him):'—he is in the central position, and possesses the requisite virtue.

42 → 27. Increase → The Corners of the Mouth (Providing Nourishment).
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject with sincere heart seeking to benefit (all below). There need be no question about it; the result will be great good fortune. (All below) will with sincere heart acknowledge his goodness.
Small Image: '(The ruler) with sincere heart seeks to benefit (all below):'—there need be no question (about the result). '(All below) with sincere heart acknowledge (his goodness):'—he gets what he desires on a great scale.

43 → 34. Break-through (Resoluteness) → The Power of the Great.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows (the small men like) a bed of purslain, which ought to be uprooted with the utmost determination. (The subject of the line having such determination), his action, in harmony with his central position, will lead to no error or blame.
Small Image: 'If his action be in harmony with his central position, there will be no error:'—but his standing in the due mean is not yet clearly displayed.

44 → 50. Coming to Meet → The Caldron.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, (shows its subject as) a medlar tree overspreading the gourd (beneath it). If he keep his brilliant qualities concealed, (a good issue) will descend (as) from Heaven.
Small Image: 'The subject of the fifth NINE, (undivided), keeps his brilliant qualities concealed:'—as is indicated by his central and correct position. '(The good issue) descends (as) from Heaven:—'his aim does not neglect the ordinances (of Heaven).

45 → 16. Gathering Together [Massing] → Enthusiasm.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows the union (of all) under its subject in the place of dignity. There will be no error. If any do not have confidence in him, let him see to it that (his virtue) be great, long-continued, and firmly correct, and all occasion for repentance will disappear.
Small Image: 'There is the union (of all) under him in the place of dignity:'—(but) his mind and aim have not yet been brilliantly displayed.

47 → 40. Oppression (Exhaustion) → Deliverance.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject with his nose and feet cut off. He is straitened by (his ministers in their) scarlet aprons. He is leisurely in his movements, however, and is satisfied. It will be well for him to be (as sincere) as in sacrificing (to spiritual beings).
Small Image: 'His nose and feet are cut off:'—his aim has not yet been gained. 'He is leisurely, however, in his movements, and is satisfied:'—his position is central and (his virtue) is correct. 'It will be well for him to be (as sincere as) in sacrificing:'— so shall he receive blessing.

48 → 46. The Well → Pushing Upward.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows a clear, limpid well, (the waters from) whose cold spring are (freely) drunk.
Small Image: 'The waters from the cold spring are (freely) drunk:'—this is indicated by the central and correct position (of the line).

49 → 55. Revolution (Molting) → Abundance.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows the great man (producing his changes) as the tiger (does when he) changes (his stripes). Before he divines (and proceeds to action), faith has been reposed in him.
Small Image: 'The great man produces his changes as the tiger does when he changes his stripes:'—their beauty becomes more brilliant.

53 → 52. Development (Gradual Progress) → Keeping Still, Mountain.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows the geese gradually advanced to the high mound. (It suggests the idea of) a wife who for three years does not become pregnant; but in the end the natural issue cannot be prevented. There will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'In the end the natural issue cannot be prevented. There will be good fortune:'—(the subject of the line) will get what he desires.

57 → 18. The Gentle (The Penetrating, Wind) → Work on what has been spoiled [Decay].
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows that with firm correctness there will be good fortune (to its subject). All occasion for repentance will disappear, and all his movements will be advantageous. There may have been no (good) beginning, but there will be a (good) end. Three days before making any changes, (let him give notice of them); and three days after, (let him reconsider them). There will (thus) be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The good fortune of (the subject of) the fifth NINE, undivided,' is owing to its correct position and its being in the centre.

58 → 54. The Joyous, Lake → The Marrying Maiden.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject trusting in one who would injure him. The situation is perilous.
Small Image: 'He trusts in one who would injure him:'—his place is that which is correct and appropriate.

59 → 4. Dispersion [Dissolution] → Youthful Folly.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject amidst the dispersion issuing his great announcements as the perspiration (flows from his body). He scatters abroad (also) the accumulations in the royal granaries. There will be no error.
Small Image: 'The accumulations of the royal (granaries) are dispersed, and there is no error:'—this is due to the correctness of the position.

60 → 19. Limitation → Approach.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject sweetly and acceptably enacting his regulations. There will be good fortune. The onward progress with them will afford ground for admiration.
Small Image: 'The good fortune arising from the regulations enacted sweetly and acceptably' is due to (the line) occupying the place (of authority) and being in the centre.

61 → 41. Inner Truth → Decrease.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject perfectly sincere, and linking (others) to him in closest union. There will be no error.
Small Image: 'He is perfectly sincere, and links others to him in closest union:'—the place (of the line) is the correct and appropriate one.

63 → 36. After Completion → Darkening of the Light.
Line: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject (as) the neighbour in the east who slaughters an ox (for his sacrifice); but this is not equal to the (small) spring sacrifice of the neighbour in the west, whose sincerity receives the blessing.
Small Image: 'The slaughtering of an ox by the neighbour in the east is not equal to (the small sacrifice of) the neighbour in the west:'—because the time (in the latter case is more important and fit). 'His sincerity receives the blessing:'—good fortune comes on a great scale.

sections.The line texts (Legge):
2 → 8. The Receptive → Holding Together [Union].
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, (shows) the yellow lower garment. There will be great good fortune.
Small Image: 'The Yellow lower-garment;—there will be great good fortune:'—this follows from that ornamental (colour's) being in the right and central place.

4 → 59. Youthful Folly → Dispersion [Dissolution].
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows its subject as a simple lad without experience. There will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The good fortune belonging to the simple lad without experience' comes from his docility going on to humility.

7 → 29. The Army → The Abysmal (Water).
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows birds in the fields, which it will be advantageous to seize (and destroy). In that case there will be no error. If the oldest son leads the host, and younger men (idly occupy offices assigned to them), however firm and correct he may be, there will be evil.
Small Image: 'The oldest son leads the host:'—its movements are directed by him in accordance with his position in the centre. 'Younger men idly occupy their positions:'—the employment of such men is improper.

11 → 5. Peace → Waiting (Nourishment).
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, reminds us of (king) Tî-yî's (rule about the) marriage of his younger sister. By such a course there is happiness and there will be great good fortune.
Small Image: 'By such a course there is happiness, and there will be great good fortune:'—(the subject of the line) employs the virtue proper to his central position to carry his wishes into effect.

14 → 1. Possession in Great Measure → The Creative.
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows the sincerity of its subject reciprocated by that of all the others (represented in the hexagram). Let him display a proper majesty, and there will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'His sincerity is reciprocated by all the others:'—his sincerity serves to stir and call out what is in their minds. 'The good fortune springing from a display of proper majesty' shows how they might (otherwise) feel too easy, and make no preparation (to serve him).

15 → 39. Modesty → Obstruction.
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows one who, without being rich, is able to employ his neighbours. He may advantageously use the force of arms. All his movements will be advantageous.
Small Image: 'He may advantageously use the force of arms:'—correcting, that is, those who do not submit.

16 → 45. Enthusiasm → Gathering Together [Massing].
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows one with a chronic complaint, but who lives on without dying.
Small Image: '(The subject of) the fifth six has a chronic complaint:'—this is shown by his being mounted on the strong (line). 'He still lives on without dying:'—he is in the central position, (and its memories of the past) have not yet perished.

18 → 57. Work on what has been spoiled [Decay] → The Gentle (The Penetrating, Wind).
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows (a son) dealing with the troubles caused by his father. He obtains the praise of using (the fit instrument for his work).
Small Image: 'He deals with the troubles caused by his father, and obtains praise:'—he is responded to (by the subject of line two) with all his virtue.

19 → 60. Approach → Limitation.
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows the advance of wisdom, such as befits the great ruler. There will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'What befits the great ruler' means the pursuing the course of the due mean.

21 → 25. Biting Through → Innocence (The Unexpected).
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows one gnawing at dried flesh, and finding the yellow gold. Let him be firm and correct, realising the peril (of his position). There will be no error.
Small Image: 'Let him be firm and correct, realising the peril (of his position), and there will be no error:'—he will possess every quality appropriate (to his position and task).

22 → 37. Grace → The Family [The Clan].
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows its subject adorned by (the occupants of) the heights and gardens. He bears his roll of silk, small and slight. He may appear stingy; but there will be good fortune in the end.
Small Image: 'The good fortune falling to the fifth six, (divided); affords occasion for joy.

23 → 20. Splitting Apart → Contemplation [View].
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows (its subject leading on the others like) a string of fishes, and (obtaining for them) the favour that lights on the inmates of the palace. There will be advantage in every way.
Small Image: 'He obtains for them the favour that lights on the inmates of the palace:'—in the end there will be no grudge against him.

24 → 3. Return (The Turning Point) → Difficulty at the Beginning.
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows the noble return of its subject. There will be no ground for repentance.
Small Image: 'The noble return, giving no ground for repentance,' is due to (the subject of the line) striving to perfect himself in accordance with his central position.

26 → 9. The Taming Power of the Great → The Taming Power of the Small.
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows the teeth of a castrated hog. There will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The good fortune indicated by the fifth six, (divided),' shows that there is occasion for congratulation.

27 → 42. The Corners of the Mouth (Providing Nourishment) → Increase.
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows one acting contrary to what is regular and proper; but if he abide in firmness, there will be good fortune. He should not, (however, try to) cross the great stream.
Small Image: 'The good fortune from abiding in firmness' is due to the docility (of the subject of the line) in following (the subject of the line) above.

30 → 13. The Clinging, Fire → Fellowship with Men.
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows its subject as one with tears flowing in torrents, and groaning in sorrow. There will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The good fortune attached to the fifth SIX, divided),' is due to its occupying the place of a king or a prince.

32 → 28. Duration → Preponderance of the Great.
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows its subject continuously maintaining the virtue indicated by it. In a wife this will be fortunate; in a husband, evil.
Small Image: 'Such firm correctness in a wife will be fortunate:'—it is hers to the end of life to follow with an unchanged mind. The husband must decide what is right, and lay down the rule accordingly:—for him to follow (like) a wife is evil.

34 → 43. The Power of the Great → Break-through (Resoluteness).
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows one who loses his ram(‐like strength) in the ease of his position. (But) there will be no occasion for repentance.
Small Image: 'He loses his ram and hardly perceives it:'—he is not in his appropriate place.

35 → 12. Progress → Standstill [Stagnation].
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows how all occasion for repentance disappears (from its subject). (But) let him not concern himself about whether he shall fail or succeed. To advance will be fortunate, and in every way advantageous.
Small Image: 'Let him not concern himself whether he fails or succeeds:'—his movement in advance will afford ground for congratulation.

36 → 63. Darkening of the Light → After Completion.
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows how the count of Kî fulfilled the condition indicated by Ming Î. It will be advantageous to be firm and correct.
Small Image: 'With the firm correctness of the count of Ki,' his brightness could not be (quite) extinguished.

38 → 10. Opposition → Treading [Conduct].
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows that (to its subject) occasion for repentance will disappear. With his relative (and minister he unites closely and readily) as if he were biting through a piece of skin. When he goes forward (with this help), what error can there be?
Small Image: 'With his hereditary minister (he unites closely and easily) as if he were biting through a piece of skin:'—his going forward will afford ground for congratulation.

40 → 47. Deliverance → Oppression (Exhaustion).
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows (its subject), the superior man (= the ruler), executing his function of removing (whatever is injurious to the idea of the hexagram), in which case there will be good fortune, and confidence in him will be shown even by the small men.
Small Image: When 'the superior man executes his function of removing (whatever is injurious to the idea of the hexagram),' small men will of themselves retire.

41 → 61. Decrease → Inner Truth.
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows parties adding to (the stores of) its subject ten pairs of tortoise shells, and accepting no refusal. There will be great good fortune.
Small Image: 'The great good fortune attached to the fifth six, (divided),' is due to the blessing from above.

46 → 48. Pushing Upward → The Well.
Line: The fifth six, divided, shows its subject firmly correct, and therefore enjoying good fortune. He ascends the stairs (with all due ceremony).
Small Image: 'He is firmly correct, and will therefore enjoy good fortune. He ascends the stairs (with all due ceremony):'—he grandly succeeds in his aim.

50 → 44. The Caldron → Coming to Meet.
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows the caldron with yellow ears and rings of metal in them. There will be advantage through being firm and correct.
Small Image: 'The caldron has yellow ears:'—the central position (of the line) is taken as (a proof of) the solid (virtue of its subject).

51 → 17. The Arousing (Shock, Thunder) → Following.
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows its subject going and coming amidst the startling movements (of the time), and always in peril; but perhaps he will not incur loss, and find business (which he can accomplish).
Small Image: 'He goes and comes amid the startling movements, and (always) in peril:'—full of risk are his doings. 'What he has to do has to be done in his central position:'—far will he be from incurring any loss.

52 → 53. Keeping Still, Mountain → Development (Gradual Progress).
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows its subject keeping his jawbones at rest, so that his words are (all) orderly. Occasion for repentance will disappear.
Small Image: 'He keeps his cheek bones at rest:'—in harmony with his central position he acts correctly.

54 → 58. The Marrying Maiden → The Joyous, Lake.
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, reminds us of the marrying of the younger sister of (king) Tî-yî, when the sleeves of her the princess were not equal to those of the (still) younger sister who accompanied her in an inferior capacity. (The case suggests the thought of) the moon almost full. There will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The sleeves of the younger sister of (king) Ti-yi, when she was married away, were not equal to those of her (half-)sister, who accompanied her:'—such was her noble character, indicated by the central position of the line.

55 → 49. Abundance → Revolution (Molting).
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows its subject bringing around him the men of brilliant ability. There will be occasion for congratulation and praise. There will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The good fortune indicated by the fifth six, (divided),'is the congratulation (that is sure to arise).

56 → 33. The Wanderer → Retreat.
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows its subject shooting a pheasant. He will lose his arrow, but in the end he will obtain praise and a (high) charge.
Small Image: 'In the end he will obtain praise and a (high) charge:'—he has reached a high place.

62 → 31. Preponderance of the Small → Influence (Wooing).
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, (suggests the idea) of dense clouds, but no rain, coming from our borders in the west. It also (shows) the prince shooting his arrow, and taking the bird in a cave.
Small Image: 'There are dense clouds, but no rain:'—(the line) is in too high a place.

64 → 6. Before Completion → Conflict.
Line: The fifth SIX, divided, shows its subject by firm correctness obtaining good fortune, and having no occasion for repentance. (We see in him) the brightness of a superior man, and the possession of sincerity. There will be good fortune.
Small Image: '(We see) the brightness of a superior man:—'the diffusion of that brightness tends to good fortune.

sections.The line texts (Legge):
1 → 44. The Creative → Coming to Meet.
Line: In the first (or lowest) NINE, undivided, (we see its subject as) the dragon lying hid (in the deep). It is not the time for active doing.
Small Image: 'The dragon lies hid in the deep;—it is not the time for active doing:'—(this appears from) the strong and undivided line's being in the lowest place.

3 → 8. Difficulty at the Beginning → Holding Together [Union].
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows the difficulty (its subject has) in advancing. It will be advantageous for him to abide correct and firm; advantageous (also) to be made a feudal ruler.
Small Image: Although 'there is a difficulty in advancing,' the mind (of the subject of the line) is set on doing what is correct. While noble, he humbles himself to the mean, and grandly gains the people.

5 → 48. Waiting (Nourishment) → The Well.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject waiting in the distant border. It will be well for him constantly to maintain (the purpose thus shown), in which case there will be no error.
Small Image: 'He is waiting in the (distant) border:'—he makes no movement to encounter rashly the difficulties (of the situation). 'It will be advantageous for him constantly to maintain (the purpose thus shown), in which case there will be no error:'—he will not fail to pursue that regular course.

9 → 57. The Taming Power of the Small → The Gentle (The Penetrating, Wind).
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject returning and pursuing his own course. What mistake should he fall into? There will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'He returns and pursues his own path:'—it is right that there should be good fortune.

10 → 6. Treading [Conduct] → Conflict.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject treading his accustomed path. If he go forward, there will be no error.
Small Image: 'He treads his accustomed path and goes forward:'—singly and exclusively he carries out his (long-cherished) wishes.

11 → 46. Peace → Pushing Upward.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, suggests the idea of grass pulled up, and bringing with it other stalks with whose roots it is connected. Advance (on the part of its subject) will be fortunate.
Small Image: 'The good fortune of advance, (as suggested by the emblem of) the grass pulled up,' arises from the will (of the party intended) being set on what is external to himself.

13 → 33. Fellowship with Men → Retreat.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, (shows the representative of) the union of men just issuing from his gate. There will be no error.
Small Image: '(The representative of) the union of men is just issuing from his gate:'—who will blame him?

14 → 50. Possession in Great Measure → The Caldron.
Line: In the first NINE, undivided, there is no approach to what is injurious, and there is no error. Let there be a realisation of the difficulty (and danger of the position), and there will be no error (to the end).
Small Image: This first NINE, (undivided),of Ta Yu shows no approach to what is injurious.

17 → 45. Following → Gathering Together [Massing].
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows us one changing the object of his pursuit; but if he be firm and correct, there will (be) good fortune. Going beyond (his own) gate to find associates, he will achieve merit.
Small Image: 'He is changing the object of his pursuit:'—but if he follow what is correct, there will be good fortune. 'He goes beyond (his own) gate to find associates:'—he will not fail (in the method he pursues).

19 → 7. Approach → The Army.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject advancing in company (with the subject of the second line). Through his firm correctness there will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The good fortune through the firm correctness of (the subject of the first line) advancing in company (with the subject of the second)' is due to his will being set on doing what is right.

21 → 35. Biting Through → Progress.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows one with his feet in the stocks and deprived of his toes. There will be no error.
Small Image: 'His feet are in the stocks, and he is deprived of his toes:'—there is no walking (to do evil).

22 → 52. Grace → Keeping Still, Mountain.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows one adorning (the way of) his feet. He can discard a carriage and walk on foot.
Small Image: 'He can discard a carriage and walk on foot:'—righteousness requires that he should not ride.

24 → 2. Return (The Turning Point) → The Receptive.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject returning (from an error) of no great extent, which would not proceed to anything requiring repentance. There will be great good fortune.
Small Image: 'Returning (from an error) of no great extent' is the prelude to the cultivation of the person.

25 → 12. Innocence (The Unexpected) → Standstill [Stagnation].
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject free from all insincerity. His advance will be accompanied with good fortune.
Small Image: When 'he who is free from insincerity makes any movement,' he will get what he desires.

26 → 18. The Taming Power of the Great → Work on what has been spoiled [Decay].
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject in a position of peril. It will be advantageous for him to stop his advance.
Small Image: 'He is in a position of peril; it will be advantageous for him to stop his advance:'—he should not rashly expose himself to calamity.

27 → 23. The Corners of the Mouth (Providing Nourishment) → Splitting Apart.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, (seems to be thus addressed), 'You leave your efficacious tortoise, and look at me till your lower jaw hangs down.' There will be evil.
Small Image: 'You look at me till your (lower) jaw hangs down:'—(the subject of the line) is thus shown unfit to be thought noble.

30 → 56. The Clinging, Fire → The Wanderer.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows one ready to move with confused steps. But he treads at the same time reverently, and there will be no mistake.
Small Image: 'The reverent attention directed to his confused steps' is the way by which error is avoided.

34 → 32. The Power of the Great → Duration.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject manifesting his strength in his toes. But advance will lead to evil,—most certainly.
Small Image: 'He manifests his vigour in his toes:'—this will certainly lead to exhaustion.

36 → 15. Darkening of the Light → Modesty.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject, (in the condition indicated by) Ming Î, flying, but with drooping wings. When the superior man (is revolving) his going away, he may be for three days without eating. Wherever he goes, the people there may speak (derisively of him).
Small Image: 'The superior man (is revolving his) going away:'—(in such a case) he feels it right not to eat.

37 → 53. The Family [The Clan] → Development (Gradual Progress).
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject establishing restrictive regulations in his household. Occasion for repentance will disappear.
Small Image: 'He establishes restrictive regulations in his household:—(he does so), before any change has taken place in their wills.

38 → 64. Opposition → Before Completion.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows that (to its subject) occasion for repentance will disappear. He has lost his horses, but let him not seek for them;—they will return of themselves. Should he meet with bad men, he will not err (in communicating with them).
Small Image: 'He meets with bad men (and communicates with them):'—(he does so), to avoid the evil of their condemnation.

41 → 4. Decrease → Youthful Folly.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject suspending his own affairs, and hurrying away (to help the subject of the fourth line). He will commit no error, but let him consider how far he should contribute of what is his (for the other).
Small Image: 'He suspends his own affairs and hurries away (to help the subject of the fourth line):'—the (subject of that) upper (line) mingles his wishes with his.

42 → 20. Increase → Contemplation [View].
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows that it will be advantageous for its subject in his position to make a great movement. If it be greatly fortunate, no blame will be imputed to him.
Small Image: 'If the movement be greatly fortunate, no blame will be imputed to him:'—though it is not for one in so low a position to have to do with great affairs.

43 → 28. Break-through (Resoluteness) → Preponderance of the Great.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject in (the pride of) strength advancing with his toes. He goes forward, but will not succeed. There will be ground for blame.
Small Image: 'Without (being able to) succeed, he goes forward:'—this is an error.

49 → 31. Revolution (Molting) → Influence (Wooing).
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject (as if he were) bound with the skin of a yellow ox.
Small Image: 'He is bound with (the skin of) a yellow ox:'—he should in his circumstances be taking action.

51 → 16. The Arousing (Shock, Thunder) → Enthusiasm.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject, when the movement approaches, looking out and around with apprehension, and afterwards smiling and talking cheerfully. There will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'When the (time of) movement comes, he will be found looking out with apprehension:'— that feeling of dread leads to happiness. 'He yet smiles and talks cheerfully:'—the issue (of his dread) is that he adopts (proper) laws (for his course).

54 → 40. The Marrying Maiden → Deliverance.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows the younger sister married off in a position ancillary to the real wife. (It suggests the idea of) a person lame on one leg who yet manages to tramp along. Going forward will be fortunate.
Small Image: 'The younger sister is married off in a position ancillary to that of the real wife:'—it is the constant practice (for such a case). 'Lame on one leg, she is able to tramp along:'—she can render helpful service.

55 → 62. Abundance → Preponderance of the Small.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject meeting with his mate. Though they are both of the same character, there will be no error. Advance will call forth approval.
Small Image: 'Though they are both of the same character, there will be no error:'—if the subject of this line seek to overpass that similarity, there will be calamity.

58 → 47. The Joyous, Lake → Oppression (Exhaustion).
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows the pleasure of (inward) harmony. There will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The good fortune attached to the pleasure of (inward) harmony' arises from there being nothing in the conduct (of the subject of the line) to awaken doubt.

60 → 29. Limitation → The Abysmal (Water).
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject not quitting the courtyard outside his door. There will be no error.
Small Image: 'He does not quit the courtyard outside his door:'—he knows when he has free course and when he is obstructed.

61 → 59. Inner Truth → Dispersion [Dissolution].
Line: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject resting (in himself). There will be good fortune. If he sought to any other, he would not find rest.
Small Image: 'The first NINE, (undivided), shows its subject resting (in himself). There will be good fortune:'—no change has yet come over his purpose.

63 → 39. After Completion → Obstruction.
Line: The first NINE, undivided, (shows its subject as a driver) who drags back his wheel, (or as a fox) which has wet his tail. There will be no error.
Small Image: 'He drags back his wheel:'—as we may rightly judge, there will be no mistake.

sections.The line texts (Legge):
2 → 24. The Receptive → Return (The Turning Point).
Line: In the first SIX, divided, (we see its subject) treading on hoarfrost. The strong ice will come (by and by).
Small Image: 'He is treading on hoarfrost;—the strong ice will come (by and by):'—the cold (air) has begun to take form. Allow it to go on quietly according to its nature, and (the hoarfrost) will come to strong ice.

4 → 41. Youthful Folly → Decrease.
Line: The first SIX, divided, (has respect to) the dispelling of ignorance. It will be advantageous to use punishment (for that purpose), and to remove the shackles (from the mind). But going on in that way (of punishment) will give occasion for regret.
Small Image: 'It will be advantageous to use punishment:'—the object being to bring under the influence of correcting law.

6 → 10. Conflict → Treading [Conduct].
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject not perpetuating the matter about which (the contention is). He will suffer the small (injury) of being spoken against, but the end will be fortunate.
Small Image: 'He does not perpetuate the matter about which (the contention is):'—contention should not be prolonged. Although 'he may suffer the small (injury) of being spoken against,' his argument is clear.

7 → 19. The Army → Approach.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows the host going forth according to the rules (for such a movement). If these be not good, there will be evil.
Small Image: 'The host goes forth according to the rules (for) such a movement:'—if those rules be not observed, there will be evil.

8 → 3. Holding Together [Union] → Difficulty at the Beginning.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject seeking by his sincerity to win the attachment of his object. There will be no error. Let (the breast) be full of sincerity as an earthenware vessel is of its contents, and it will in the end bring other advantages.
Small Image: From 'the seeking union with its object' shown in the first SIX, (divided),there will be other advantages.

12 → 25. Standstill [Stagnation] → Innocence (The Unexpected).
Line: The first SIX, divided, suggests the idea of grass pulled up, and bringing with it other stalks with whose roots it is connected. With firm correctness (on the part of its subject), there will be good fortune and progress.
Small Image: 'The good fortune through firm goodness, (suggested by) the pulling up of the grass,' arises from the will (of the parties intended) being bent on (serving) the ruler.

15 → 36. Modesty → Darkening of the Light.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows us the superior man who adds humility to humility. (Even) the great stream may be crossed with this, and there will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The superior man who adds humility to humility' is one who nourishes his (virtue) in lowliness.

16 → 51. Enthusiasm → The Arousing (Shock, Thunder).
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject proclaiming his pleasure and satisfaction. There will be evil.
Small Image: 'The (subject of the) first six proclaims his pleasure and satisfaction:'—there will be evil; his wishes have been satisfied to overflowing.

18 → 26. Work on what has been spoiled [Decay] → The Taming Power of the Great.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows (a son) dealing with the troubles caused by his father. If he be an (able) son, the father will escape the blame of having erred. The position is perilous, but there will be good fortune in the end.
Small Image: 'He deals with the troubles caused by his father:'—he feels that he has entered into the work of his father.

20 → 42. Contemplation [View] → Increase.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows the looking of a lad;—not blamable in men of inferior rank, but matter for regret in superior men.
Small Image: 'The looking of a lad shown by the first six, (divided); indicates the way of the inferior people.

23 → 27. Splitting Apart → The Corners of the Mouth (Providing Nourishment).
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows one overturning the couch by injuring its legs. (The injury will go on to) the destruction of (all) firm correctness, and there will be evil.
Small Image: 'He overthrows the couch by injuring its legs:'—thus (he commences) his work of ruin with what is lowest (in the superior man).

28 → 43. Preponderance of the Great → Break-through (Resoluteness).
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows one placing mats of the white mâo grass under things set on the ground. There will be no error.
Small Image: 'He places mats of the white mao grass under things set on the ground:'—he feels his weakness and his being in the lowest place, (and uses extraordinary care).

29 → 60. The Abysmal (Water) → Limitation.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject in the double defile, and (yet) entering a cavern within it. There will be evil.
Small Image: 'In the double defile, he enters a cavern within it:'—he has missed his (proper) way, and there will be evil.

31 → 49. Influence (Wooing) → Revolution (Molting).
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows one moving his great toes.
Small Image: 'He moves his great toe:'—his mind is set on what is beyond (himself).

32 → 34. Duration → The Power of the Great.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject deeply (desirous) of long continuance. Even with firm correctness there will be evil; there will be no advantage in any way.
Small Image: 'The evil attached to the deep desire for long continuance (in the subject of the first line)' arises from the deep seeking for it at the commencement (of things).

33 → 13. Retreat → Fellowship with Men.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows a retiring tail. The position is perilous. No movement in any direction should be made.
Small Image: There is 'the perilousness of the position shown by the retiring tail:'—but if 'no movement' be made, what disaster can there be?

35 → 21. Progress → Biting Through.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows one wishing to advance, and (at the same time) kept back. Let him be firm and correct, and there will be good fortune. If trust be not reposed in him, let him maintain a large and generous mind, and there will be no error.
Small Image: 'He appears wishing to advance, but (at the same time) being kept back:'—all-alone he pursues the correct course. 'Let him maintain a large and generous mind, and there will be no error:'—he has not yet received an official charge.

39 → 63. Obstruction → After Completion.
Line: From the first SIX, divided, we learn that advance (on the part of its subject) will lead to (greater) difficulties, while remaining stationary will afford ground for praise.
Small Image: 'Advancing will conduct to (greater) difficulties, while remaining stationary will afford ground for praise:'—the proper course is to wait.

40 → 54. Deliverance → The Marrying Maiden.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows that its subject will commit no error.
Small Image: The strong (fourth) line and the weak line here are in correlation:—we judge rightly in saying that 'its subject will commit no error.'

44 → 1. Coming to Meet → The Creative.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows how its subject should be kept (like a carriage) tied and fastened to a metal drag, in which case with firm correctness there will be good fortune. (But) if he move in any direction, evil will appear. He will be (like) a lean pig, which is sure to keep jumping about.
Small Image: 'Tied and fastened to a metal drag:'—(this describes the arrest of) the weak (line) in its advancing course.

45 → 17. Gathering Together [Massing] → Following.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject with a sincere desire (for union), but unable to carry it out, so that disorder is brought into the sphere of his union. If he cry out (for help to his proper correlate), all at once (his tears) will give place to smiles. He need not mind (the temporary difficulty); as he goes forward, there will be no error.
Small Image: 'In consequence disorder is brought into the sphere of his union:'—his mind and aim are thrown into confusion.

46 → 11. Pushing Upward → Peace.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject advancing upwards with the welcome (of those above him). There will be great good fortune.
Small Image: 'He is welcomed in his advance upwards, and there will be great good fortune:'—(the subjects of) the upper (trigram) are of the same mind with him.

47 → 58. Oppression (Exhaustion) → The Joyous, Lake.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject with bare buttocks straitened under the stump of a tree. He enters a dark valley, and for three years has no prospect (of deliverance).
Small Image: 'He enters a dark valley:'—so benighted is he, and without clear vision.

48 → 5. The Well → Waiting (Nourishment).
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows a well so muddy that men will not drink of it; or an old well to which neither birds (nor other creatures) resort.
Small Image: 'A well so muddy that men will not drink of it:'—this is indicated by the low position (of the line). 'An old well to which the birds do not come:'—it has been forsaken in the course of time.

50 → 14. The Caldron → Possession in Great Measure.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows the caldron overthrown and its feet turned up. (But) there will be advantage in its getting rid of what was bad in it. (Or it shows us) the concubine (whose position is improved) by means of her son. There will be no error.
Small Image: 'The caldron is overturned, and its feet turned upwards:'—but this is not (all) contrary (to what is right). 'There will be advantage in getting rid of what was bad:'—thereby (the subject of the line) will follow the more noble (subject of the fourth line).

52 → 22. Keeping Still, Mountain → Grace.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject keeping his toes at rest. There will be no error; but it will be advantageous for him to be persistently firm and correct.
Small Image: 'He keeps his toes at rest:'—he does not fail in what is correct (according to the idea of the figure).

53 → 37. Development (Gradual Progress) → The Family [The Clan].
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows the wild geese gradually approaching the shore. A young officer (in similar circumstances) will be in a position of danger, and be spoken against; but there will be no error.
Small Image: 'The danger of a small officer (as represented in the first line)' is owing to no fault of his in the matter of what is right.

56 → 30. The Wanderer → The Clinging, Fire.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows the stranger mean and meanly occupied. It is thus that he brings on himself (further) calamity.
Small Image: 'The stranger is mean and meanly occupied:'—his aim is become of the lowest character, and calamity will ensue.

57 → 9. The Gentle (The Penetrating, Wind) → The Taming Power of the Small.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject (now) advancing, (now) receding. It would be advantageous for him to have the firm correctness of a brave soldier.
Small Image: '(Now) he advances, (now) he recedes:'—his mind is perplexed. It would be advantageous for him to have the firmness of a brave soldier:'—his mind would in that case be well governed.

59 → 61. Dispersion [Dissolution] → Inner Truth.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject engaged in rescuing (from the impending evil) and having (the assistance of) a strong horse. There will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The good fortune attached to the first six, divided),'is due to the natural course (pursued by its subject).

62 → 55. Preponderance of the Small → Abundance.
Line: The first SIX, divided, suggests (the idea of) a bird flying, (and ascending) till the issue is evil.
Small Image: 'There is a bird flying (and ascending) till the result is evil:'—nothing can be done to avoid this issue.

64 → 38. Before Completion → Opposition.
Line: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject (like a fox) whose tail gets immersed. There will be occasion for regret.
Small Image: 'His tail gets immersed:'—this is the very height of ignorance.

sections.The line texts (Legge):
1 → 13. The Creative → Fellowship with Men.
Line: In the second NINE, undivided, (we see its subject as) the dragon appearing in the field. It will be advantageous to meet with the great man.
Small Image: 'The dragon appears in the field:'—the diffusion of virtuous influence has been wide.

4 → 23. Youthful Folly → Splitting Apart.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, (shows its subject) exercising forbearance with the ignorant, in which there will be good fortune; and admitting (even the goodness of women, which will also be fortunate). (He may be described also as) a son able to (sustain the burden of) his family.
Small Image: 'A son able to (sustain the burden of) his family:'—as appears from the reciprocation between this strong line and the weak (fifth line).

5 → 63. Waiting (Nourishment) → After Completion.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject waiting on the sand (of the mountain stream). He will (suffer) the small (injury of) being spoken (against), but in the end there will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'He is waiting on the sand:'—he occupies his position in the centre with a generous forbearance. Though 'he suffer the small injury of being spoken (against),' he will bring things to a good issue.

6 → 12. Conflict → Standstill [Stagnation].
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject unequal to the contention. If he retire and keep concealed (where) the inhabitants of his city are (only) three hundred families, he will fall into no mistake.
Small Image: 'He is unequal to the contention; he retires and keeps concealed, stealthily withdrawing from it:'—for him from his lower place to contend with (the stronger one) above, would be to (invite) calamity, as if he brought it with his hand to himself.

7 → 2. The Army → The Receptive.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows (the leader) in the midst of the host. There will be good fortune and no error. The king has thrice conveyed to him the orders (of his favour).
Small Image: 'He is in the midst of the host, and there will be good fortune:'—he has received the favour of Heaven. 'The king has thrice conveyed to him the orders (of) his favour:'—(the king) cherishes the myriad regions in his heart.

9 → 37. The Taming Power of the Small → The Family [The Clan].
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject, by the attraction (of the former line), returning (to the proper course). There will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'By the attraction (of the subject of the former line) he returns (to its own course),' and is in the central place:—neither will he err in what is due from him.

10 → 25. Treading [Conduct] → Innocence (The Unexpected).
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject treading the path that is level and easy;—a quiet and solitary man, to whom, if he be firm and correct, there will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'A quiet and solitary man, to whom, being firm and correct, there will be good fortune:'—holding the due mean, he will not allow himself to be thrown into disorder.

11 → 36. Peace → Darkening of the Light.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows one who can bear with the uncultivated, will cross the Ho without a boat, does not forget the distant, and has no (selfish) friendships. Thus does he prove himself acting in accordance with the course of the due Mean.
Small Image: 'He bears with the uncultivated, and proves himself acting in accordance with the due mean:'—for (his intelligence is) bright and (his capacity is) great.

14 → 30. Possession in Great Measure → The Clinging, Fire.
Line: In the second NINE, undivided, we have a large waggon with its load. In whatever direction advance is made, there will be no error.
Small Image: 'A large waggon with its load' refers to the (virtue) accumulated (in the subject of the line), so that he will suffer no loss (in the conduct of affairs).

18 → 52. Work on what has been spoiled [Decay] → Keeping Still, Mountain.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows (a son) dealing with the troubles caused by his mother. He should not (carry) his firm correctness (to the utmost).
Small Image: 'He deals with the troubles caused by his mother:'—he holds to the course of the due mean.

19 → 24. Approach → Return (The Turning Point).
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject advancing in company (with the subject of the first line). There will be good fortune; advancing will be in every way advantageous.
Small Image: 'The good fortune and every possible advantage attending the advance (of the subject of the second line), in company (with the subject of the first),' arises from the fact that those (to whom the advance is made) are not yet obedient to the ordinances (of Heaven).

26 → 22. The Taming Power of the Great → Grace.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows a carriage with the strap under it removed.
Small Image: '(He is as) a carriage from which the strap under it has been removed:'—being in the central position, he will incur no blame.

28 → 31. Preponderance of the Great → Influence (Wooing).
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows a decayed willow producing shoots, or an old husband in possession of his young wife. There will be advantage in every way.
Small Image: 'An old husband and a young wife:'—such association is extraordinary.

29 → 8. The Abysmal (Water) → Holding Together [Union].
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject in all the peril of the defile. He will, however, get a little (of the deliverance) that he seeks.
Small Image: 'He will get a little (of the deliverance) that he seeks:'—he will not yet escape from his environed position.

32 → 62. Duration → Preponderance of the Small.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows all occasion for repentance disappearing.
Small Image: 'All occasion for repentance on the part of the subject of the second NINE, (undivided,), disappears:'—he can abide long in the due mean.

34 → 55. The Power of the Great → Abundance.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows that with firm correctness there will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The second NINE, (undivided), shows that with firm correctness there will be good fortune:'—this is due to its being in the centre, (and its subject exemplifying the due mean).

38 → 21. Opposition → Biting Through.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject happening to meet with his lord in a bye‐passage. There will be no error.
Small Image: 'He happens to meet with his lord in a bye-passage:'—but he has not deviated (for this meeting) from the (proper) course.

40 → 16. Deliverance → Enthusiasm.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject catch, in hunting, three foxes, and obtain the yellow (= golden) arrows. With firm correctness there will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The good fortune springing from the firm correctness of the second NINE, (undivided),' is due to its subject holding the due mean.

41 → 27. Decrease → The Corners of the Mouth (Providing Nourishment).
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows that it will be advantageous for its subject to maintain a firm correctness, and that action on his part will be evil. He can give increase (to his correlate) without taking from himself.
Small Image: 'It will be advantageous for (the subject of) the second NINE, (undivided), to maintain his firm correctness:'—his central position gives its character to his aim.

43 → 49. Break-through (Resoluteness) → Revolution (Molting).
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject full of apprehension and appealing (for sympathy and help). Late at night hostile measures may be (taken against him), but he need not be anxious about them.
Small Image: 'Though hostile measures be taken against him, he need not be anxious:'—he pursues the course of the due mean.

44 → 33. Coming to Meet → Retreat.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject with a wallet of fish. There will be no error. But it will not be well to let (the subject of the first line) go forward to the guests.
Small Image: 'He has a wallet of fish:'—it is right for him not to allow (the subject of the first line) to get to the guests.

46 → 15. Pushing Upward → Modesty.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject with that sincerity which will make even the (small) offerings of the vernal sacrifice acceptable. There will be no error.
Small Image: 'The sincerity of the subject of the second NINE, undivided,' affords occasion for joy.

47 → 45. Oppression (Exhaustion) → Gathering Together [Massing].
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject straitened amidst his wine and viands. There come to him anon the red knee-covers (of the ruler). It will be well for him (to maintain his sincerity as) in sacrificing. Active operations (on his part) will lead to evil, but he will be free from blame.
Small Image: 'He is straitened amidst his wine and viands:'—(but) his position is central, and there will be ground for congratulation.

48 → 39. The Well → Obstruction.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows a well from which by a hole the water escapes and flows away to the shrimps (and such small creatures among the grass), or one the water of which leaks away from a broken basket.
Small Image: 'A well from which by a hole the water escapes, and flows away to the shrimps:'—(the subject of this second line has) none co-operating with him (above).

50 → 56. The Caldron → The Wanderer.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows the caldron with the things (to be cooked) in it. (If its subject can say), 'My enemy dislikes me, but he cannot approach me,' there will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'There is the caldron with the things (to be cooked) in it:'—let (the subject of the line) be careful where he goes. 'My enemy dislikes me:'—but there will in the end be no fault (to which he can point).

54 → 51. The Marrying Maiden → The Arousing (Shock, Thunder).
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows her blind of one eye, and yet able to see. There will be advantage in her maintaining the firm correctness of a solitary widow.
Small Image: 'There will be advantage in maintaining the firm correctness of a solitary widow:'—(the subject of the line) has not changed from the constancy (proper to a wife).

57 → 53. The Gentle (The Penetrating, Wind) → Development (Gradual Progress).
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows the representative of Sun beneath a couch, and employing diviners and exorcists in a way bordering on confusion. There will be good fortune and no error.
Small Image: 'The good fortune springing from what borders on confusion' is due to the position (of the line) in the centre.

58 → 17. The Joyous, Lake → Following.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows the pleasure arising from (inward) sincerity. There will be good fortune. Occasion for repentance will disappear.
Small Image: 'The good fortune attached to the pleasure arising from (inward sincerity)' is due to the confidence felt in the object (of the subject of the line).

59 → 20. Dispersion [Dissolution] → Contemplation [View].
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject, amid the dispersion, hurrying to his contrivance (for security). All occasion for repentance will disappear.
Small Image: 'Amidst the prevailing dispersion, he hurries to his contrivance (for security):'—he gets what he desires.

60 → 3. Limitation → Difficulty at the Beginning.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject not quitting the courtyard inside his gate. There will be evil.
Small Image: 'He does not quit the courtyard inside his gate. There will be evil:'—he loses the time (for action) to an extreme degree.

61 → 42. Inner Truth → Increase.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject (like) the crane crying out in her hidden retirement, and her young ones responding to her. (It is as if it were said), 'I have a cup of good spirits,' (and the response were), 'I will partake of it with you.'
Small Image: 'Her young ones respond to her:'—from the (common) wish of the inmost heart.

64 → 35. Before Completion → Progress.
Line: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject dragging back his (carriage-) wheel. With firmness and correctness there will be good fortune.
Small Image: 'The second NINE, (undivided), shows good fortune arising from being firm and correct:'—it is in the central place, and the action of its subject thereby becomes correct.
